Shares of Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) fell 20.2% between October 9 and October 15, 2026. The decline included an 8.3% drop on October 14 and a further 7.1% drop on October 15. A rapid decline tempts buyers who expect a rebound and who trust the company to keep turning orders for AI systems and traditional servers into sales. So how did people who bought HPE's earlier falls do?

HPE Stock Was Higher A Year After Past Falls

HPE stock has closed more than 20% below its level of 30 trading days earlier on nine occasions since November 2015. Eight of those declines occurred over a year ago, and the stock was higher a year later in every instance. Buyers saw a median gain of 29.5% over that year. The ninth fall took place in November 2025 and remains too recent to judge.

Realizing those gains required patience. In the median case, the stock's lowest close in the following year was 8.6% below its close on the day of the initial fall. After the March 2025 drop, the stock closed as much as 33.2% lower before climbing to be up 17% a year later. The highest price within each year arrived a median 317 days after the decline. Buyers waited about ten months to see that peak.

Is HPE Still Turning Orders Into Sales?

The company is doing just that, though not as fast as customers are ordering. Revenue grew 33.7% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026, which ended July 31, while operating profit expanded even faster. Part of the revenue growth came from HPE's acquisition of Juniper Networks. On management's figures, which count Juniper in both years, networking revenue grew 10%. The operating margin reached 12.0%, compared to 4.7% in the same quarter a year earlier. Cash from operations accounted for 13.4% of revenue, standing close to the 13.2% recorded the previous quarter.

This story was originally published on CFO.com. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CFO.com newsletter.

Mark Long | Super Micro Computer

Super Micro Computer appointed Mark Long as the AI server maker's new senior vice president and chief financial officer. Long's earlier roles include co-founder and partner of investment firm Prime Impact Capital, senior adviser of McKinsey & Company and CFO and chief strategy officer of Western Digital. Long succeeds David Weigand, who has been CFO since February 2021. In December 2024, Super Micro said it would search for a new CFO as part of recommendations from an independent special committee that reviewed its accounting practices. The committee was formed after EY abruptly resigned as Super Micro's auditor, saying it questioned whether the firm was "committed to integrity and ethical values." The final investigation findings noted there was no management misconduct, but there were "lapses" regarding rehiring former employees who previously resigned after a 2017 audit committee investigation. 

Jeff Schrader | Sierra Space

Jeff Schrader, CFO of Sierra Space, has left the spacecraft maker to pursue a new professional opportunity, according to Bloomberg reporting. Schrader joined the company in March as chief strategy officer from Lockheed Martin Space, and took over as Sierra Space's chief financial officer in June. Schrader started his career as a U.S. Air Force financial analyst, advancing to CFO for special programs and later the Air Force Rapid Capabilities Office. Schrader's departure brings questions about the timing of Sierra Space's long-awaited IPO, which the company has been discussing since 2024. 

Joseph Sesin | Denver Broncos

Joseph Sesin was named finance chief of the Denver Broncos. Sesin joins the NFL team from Angel City Football Club of the National Women's Soccer League, where he was most recently senior vice president of finance and accounting. Before that, he was senior vice president of accounting and finance for SoFi Stadium, YouTube Theater and Hollywood Park in Los Angeles. He started his career at J.P. Morgan, where he worked for over eight years, most recently as vice president. Sesin succeeds longtime CFO Justin Webster, who left in August. Webster joined the organization in 2010 and took over as chief financial officer in 2013. 

Anne Giviskos | MoonPay

Anne Giviskos was appointed finance chief of MoonPay, a global financial technology firm that provides payment and trading infrastructure for digital assets. Giviskos was most recently interim CFO and chief accounting officer at business travel and expense platform Navan. Earlier roles include chief risk and compliance officer at Euronext and director of finance at the New York Stock Exchange.

title: Super Micro’s CFO is out after change was slow-walked

Super Micro’s CFO is out after change was slow-walked

This story was originally published on CFO Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CFO Dive newsletter.

Dive Brief:

San Jose, California-based Super Micro Computer said Thursday that long-time CFO David Weigand stepped down from the post, effective immediately, according to a press release and securities filing. 

The AI server maker, which was advised by an independent special committee to hire a new finance chief in 2024 after "lapses" in certain processes were identified, appointed former Western Digital CFO Mark Long to succeed Weigand. The outgoing CFO has served as finance chief since 2021, according to his LinkedIn. 

Charles Liang, the company's founder, president, and CEO, cited Long's strategic expertise in a statement in the release. "I'm confident Mark will have an immediate positive impact in strengthening and accelerating our operational and financial execution as we continue to scale our business to capture the next wave of AI and IT infrastructure growth," Liang said. 

Dive Insight:

The financial leadership change comes as the high-flying AI darling has wrestled with serious legal and compliance issues. 

In May, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called out the company, asserting that its partner needed to strengthen its export compliance controls. In response to news that Taiwan had detained three people for allegedly making fraudulent declarations about AI servers made by SMC, Huang said he hoped Super Micro "will enhance and improve their regulation compliance and avoid that from happening in the future," Bloomberg reported. 

In a statement at the time, Super Micro asserted that the events underscored the need for "industry-wide solutions that would further help safeguard supply chains and strengthen enforcement of export control laws," CFO Dive previously reported.  

The rebuke from Nvidia's CEO came after Super Micro's co-founder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw, another executive and a contractor — all no longer affiliated with the company — were indicted in March in the U.S. in connection with a smuggling scheme involving billions of dollars of servers with AI chips diverted to China. In April the company, which was not named as a defendant in the indictment, launched an independent investigation into the indictments.

Meanwhile, Super Micro's protracted internal control repairs have also drawn criticism, including from accounting academics, as its efforts to fix weaknesses in its internal financial controls have dragged into a second year.

title: Supermicro promised a new CFO in December 2024. A $2.5 billion smuggling case and a cofounder’s arrest later, it has one

Supermicro promised a new CFO in December 2024. A $2.5 billion smuggling case and a cofounder’s arrest later, it has one
Charles Liang, CEO of Super Micro Computer · Fortune · Nathan Laine—Bloomberg/Getty Images

WDC

SPCX

Super Micro Computer, the troubled hardware ally of Nvidia and Elon Musk's SpaceX, has finally hired a new head of finance. The appointment comes nearly two years after a board-level independent investigation led the company to commit to "immediately" begin searching for a replacement for longtime chief financial officer David Weigand.

Mark Long, 59, replaced Weigand as CFO on Wednesday—"effective immediately," according to Supermicro—and he brings with him a stack of bona fides. He previously served as CFO and chief strategy officer at $130 billion data storage company Western Digital, and he runs an investment and advisory firm, Prime Impact Capital. Long also served a stint as co-CEO and CFO of a SPAC he cofounded that raised $300 million before it merged in 2023 with a Beijing-based auto insurance technology platform, Cheche Technology.

He joins Supermicro at an incredibly complex moment for the hardware maker with deep ties to Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, and Musk's xAI, which was folded into SpaceX. Long's record as a veteran executive and tech investor is likely intended to help clear the cloud that has hovered over Supermicro for the past two years and to burnish its credibility with skeptical investors.

In March, the Department of Justice and FBI indicted and arrested Supermicro cofounder Yih-Shyan "Wally" Liaw in a shocking smuggling case allegedly involving $2.5 billion of Supermicro hardware loaded with Nvidia's export-controlled chips being illegally routed to China. Liaw, along with two others associated with Supermicro, was alleged to have gone to extreme lengths to deceive officials, including using hair dryers to remove and replace sticky labels and staging thousands of dummy servers that were nonworking physical replicas of actual Supermicro servers—because the real servers had already been diverted to China.

Supermicro is not named as a defendant in the case, and has said it is cooperating with law enforcement. Liaw has pleaded not guilty. His March arrest, however, kicked off another board-led internal investigation—separate from the previous probe that led to the CFO search—that Supermicro said in August found no evidence that current members of senior management knew about the smuggling scheme. 

Until he resigned after being arrested and charged in the smuggling case, Liaw had served on the Supermicro board and had a long history with fellow cofounders Charles Liang and Sara Liu. (Liu and Liang are married and both serve on the Supermicro board.) Liaw had previously left Supermicro in the midst of an internal audit committee investigation just before a 2018 SEC probe charged Supermicro and its then-CFO with improper revenue recognition practices. Supermicro settled the SEC's charges and paid a $17.5 million settlement in 2020. Liaw returned to Supermicro as a consultant in May 2021 and eventually became a full-time employee before rejoining the board in December 2023.

SAN JOSE, Calif., October 15, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Super Micro Computer, Inc. (Nasdaq: SMCI), an AI, Enterprise, Storage, and 5G/Edge Total IT Solution Provider featuring Data Center Building Block Solutions® (DCBBS), today announced the appointment of Mark Long as Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer reporting directly to the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Charles Liang, effective immediately.

Mr. Long is a seasoned finance executive with decades of experience across the technology sector spanning corporate finance, strategy, mergers and acquisitions, and capital allocation. He previously served as Chief Financial Officer and Chief Strategy Officer of Western Digital, where he led financial management, investor relations and corporate strategy, and played a central role in building a scaled, global data infrastructure leader. Mr. Long previously served as co-founder and Partner of Prime Impact Capital, a technology-focused investment firm, was a Senior Vice President of Strategy and Corporate Development at Hitachi Global Storage Technologies and, earlier in his career, held senior roles in investment banking focused on the software, cloud infrastructure, and storage sectors.

"We are pleased to welcome Mark to the Supermicro executive team and look forward to benefitting from his deep strategic expertise and proven leadership," said Charles Liang, Founder, President, and CEO of Supermicro. "I'm confident Mark will have an immediate positive impact in strengthening and accelerating our operational and financial execution as we continue to scale our business to capture the next wave of AI and IT infrastructure growth."

Liang continued, "We are also grateful to David Weigand for his many years of service as CFO and for his support of an orderly transition."

"I am honored to join Supermicro as it continues to build on its leadership in AI and high-performance infrastructure," said Mr. Long. "Charles has built a remarkable company, and I look forward to partnering closely with him and the executive team to scale the business effectively and efficiently – strengthening our financial foundation while supporting continued innovation, growth, and long-term value creation for shareholders."

The company conducted an extensive search process to identify and secure an exceptional candidate with the necessary skills and experience. Mr. Long succeeds David Weigand. David will assist in the transition and shift his focus to helping optimize and accelerate the business.

title: Is SMCI Stock A Real Bargain?
detail:
Is SMCI Stock A Real Bargain?
Trefis Team
Thu, October 15, 2026 at 5:52 AM MST 3 min read
SMCI
DELL
HPE
ANET
CSCO
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

Shares of Super Micro Computer (SMCI) trade at 9.8 times earnings. The median S&P 500 company trades at 22.7. Over the past year, Super Micro stock lost 34.6%, while the broader index returned 17.3%. This low price could point to a fast-growing server maker on sale, or it might reflect a fair price for profits that may not turn into cash. So does Super Micro's profit back up the low price?

Super Micro's Profit Has More Than Doubled

The company earned $2.23 billion in the twelve months to June 2026, compared with $1.05 billion a year earlier. Revenue grew 77.8% over those twelve months, while the median S&P 500 company grew 8.3%. Super Micro sells mainly servers: server and storage systems made up 97% of its revenue in fiscal 2025, the twelve months to June 2025.

Super Micro has maintained its operating margin during this rapid expansion. Operating margin was 7.1% over the twelve months to June 2026, roughly in line with its 7.0% average over the three latest twelve-month periods. Gross margin was 10.8% over the same twelve months, below its 11.9% average. The low P/E is not a discount on shrinking profit.

Did Super Micro's Operations Bring In Money?

No. Over the same twelve months, Super Micro's operations used $6.81 billion of cash. A year earlier, they brought in $1.66 billion. A single quarter accounted for most of the outflow, with operations using $6.62 billion from January to March 2026.

Super Micro has used cash during periods of rapid growth before. In the twelve months to June 2024, when revenue more than doubled, its operations used $2.49 billion of cash. In two of the last three years, Super Micro reported a profit while its operations paid out more cash than they took in.

Inflow Returned From April To June, But Debt Grew

After three quarters in which they used cash, Super Micro's operations brought in $747 million of cash from April to June 2026. This inflow remained below the $864 million recorded in the same quarter a year earlier. Sales from April to June 2026 nearly doubled from a year earlier, and cash came in alongside the growth. Each dollar of sales also kept more profit: gross margin was 17.5% that quarter, compared with 9.5% in the same quarter a year earlier.

The company also carries more debt than it did a year ago. Total debt was $8.76 billion at June 30, 2026, up from $4.78 billion a year earlier. On the same date, it held $7.52 billion of cash and short-term investments. A P/E counts only earnings, leaving out both the debt and the cash.

Super Micro is growing its profit, but whether that profit arrives as cash remains an open question after one good quarter. A buyer at this price is betting that Super Micro can keep its operations bringing in cash, not that the market has misjudged a healthy business. The crucial metric to watch is cash from operations for the July to September 2026 quarter, detailed in the report expected on or around November 3, 2026. Seeing cash come in again would support the bet, while a return to using cash would undercut it.
